scenes.spec: cold morning, car starting, white vapor puffing from tailpipe
scenes.narration: You start the car, glance in the mirror, and there it is — a white cloud rolling out of the exhaust. And your brain immediately offers you the two scariest words in car ownership: *head gasket*. Here's the thing: sometimes white smoke IS that. And most of the time, it's literally just weather. The difference between "nothing" and "the most expensive repair on the menu" comes down to three things you can check in your driveway in five minutes, for free. Let's make sure you never pay for a diagnosis you could've done with your own eyes.

scenes.spec: channel card — "Why Is My Car Doing That?"
three-way split — "Disappears after warm-up?" / "Sweet smell?" / "Coolant level dropping?"
scenes.narration: Three driveway checks, in order. **One: does it stop?** Vapor on a cold morning that thins out and disappears within a few minutes of driving is one thing. White smoke that keeps pouring out of a fully warmed-up engine is another entirely. **Two: smell it.** Carefully, from a respectful distance. Real coolant-smoke has a distinctive **sweet** smell — antifreeze has sugar- adjacent chemistry, and burning it smells like syrup gone wrong. Water vapor smells like nothing. **Three: check the coolant.** Engine COLD — never open a hot cooling system, that's a face full of boiling coolant waiting to happen — look at the overflow tank level. Mark it with tape. Check again in a week. Smoke plus a *dropping* level is a story. Smoke with a rock-steady level usually isn't. scenes.section: THE MECHANISM — WHAT WHITE SMOKE ACTUALLY IS
scenes.spec: NEW 3D — engine block section: combustion chambers, coolant jackets surrounding them, head gasket as the sealing plane between
scenes.narration: White exhaust smoke is **steam** — water becoming vapor in a hot place it doesn't belong. To understand every cause in this episode, you need one picture: inside your engine, combustion and coolant live millimeters apart, separated by gaskets and castings. The **combustion chambers** burn fuel. Wrapped around them, the **coolant jackets** carry away heat. Between them, sealing the deal, sits the **head gasket** — a precision sandwich layer clamped between the engine block and the cylinder head. Water in the exhaust means water crossed a boundary somewhere — or was just condensation that never crossed anything at all. Ranked, from overwhelmingly-common to genuinely-serious:

scenes.section: CAUSE #1 — CONDENSATION: THE MORNING FOG (most common, zero cost)
scenes.spec: exhaust pipe cross-section overnight — moist air condensing on cool metal, morning start flash-boiling it to vapor
scenes.narration: Your exhaust system is a long metal tube that cools overnight. Air inside it condenses moisture onto the metal — same reason your lawn has dew. First start of the day, hot exhaust gas hits those wet walls and flash-boils the condensation into a white puff that lasts... about as long as the water does. Thirty seconds to a few minutes, thinner as the pipes warm, gone. Cold climates, short trips, and humid nights make it more dramatic. It's not a malfunction. It's a kettle. If your white smoke passes the three-check test — stops after warm-up, no smell, coolant steady — close this video and have a good day. That's most of you. scenes.section: CAUSE #2 — A FAILING HEAD GASKET (the famous one)
scenes.spec: head gasket plane — breach path drawn from coolant jacket into combustion chamber, steam exiting exhaust valve
scenes.narration: The one everyone fears, so let's be precise about what it actually is. The head gasket seals three different things from each other: combustion pressure, coolant passages, and oil passages. When the seal breaches between a **coolant passage and a combustion chamber**, coolant seeps into the cylinder and gets steamed out the exhaust — continuously, warm or cold, with that sweet smell, while the overflow tank slowly drops. Supporting evidence to look for: gasket in the first place [TECH CONFIRM — in your bays, is overheating usually the cause of the gasket failure, the result, or both?] gas pushing the other way through the breach finding its way into oil (though short-trip condensation can fake this one) [TECH CONFIRM — how do you tell milky-cap-from-short-trips vs milky-cap-from-gasket at the counter?] A modern shop confirms with a **block test** — a chemical sniffer that detects combustion gases in the coolant [TECH CONFIRM — is the block test your standard confirm, or compression/leak-down first?].

scenes.section: CAUSE #3 — A CRACKED HEAD OR BLOCK (the same story, worse edition)
scenes.spec: cylinder head with hairline crack propagating between coolant passage and chamber
scenes.narration: Same symptoms as the head gasket — because it's the same *leak*, through a crack in the metal castings instead of the gasket between them. Usually the aftermath of serious overheating: aluminum heads especially warp and crack when cooked. The reason it matters: a gasket is a part, a cracked head is a component, and a cracked block is a decision about the whole car. You can't tell which one you have from the driveway — that's teardown territory — but the driveway evidence that points HERE rather than at the gasket is a history of *repeated* or *severe* overheating.

scenes.spec: injector spraying into chamber, unburnt fuel mist exiting as white-gray smoke
scenes.narration: Worth a lane of its own: on diesels, white-gray smoke often isn't water at all — it's **unburnt fuel** from glow plug problems, injector timing, or low compression on cold starts. Smells like fuel, not syrup. If you drive a diesel, the sweet-smell check matters double, because the white-smoke decision tree forks completely. scenes.section: THE REPAIR — WHAT THE MONEY LOOKS LIKE
scenes.spec: decision tree — three-check test in, outcomes out
scenes.narration: labor — the head comes off, gets checked for flatness, machined if needed, new gasket, reassembly, and always a hunt for WHY it failed (usually a cooling-system problem that's also on the bill). On older, higher-mileage cars this is where repair-vs-replace-the-car math enters the room — a conversation an honest shop will have with you straight. scenes.spec: three-tier verdict card — "It's weather" / "Book the block test" / "Stop driving"
scenes.narration: **It's weather:** morning vapor, gone in minutes, no smell, steady coolant. Zero action. **Book the block test:** persistent smoke, sweet smell, or a coolant level that drops week over week — even slowly. Days-to-a-couple-weeks urgency: the breach only grows, and coolant loss is how the next tier happens. **Stop driving:** smoke plus a climbing temperature gauge, plus rough running, or plus the low-coolant light. Driving an overheating engine with a coolant breach is how gaskets become heads and heads become engines — the tow is the cheapest part you'll buy all year. [TECH CONFIRM — bless the tiers]

So: white smoke that quits after warm-up is a kettle, not a car problem. Persistent sweet-smelling smoke with a thirsty coolant tank is a breach between the wet side and the fire side — gasket if you're lucky, casting if you're not. And the three-check driveway test — warm-up, smell, coolant level — sorts almost everyone into the right line for free.
